title: I Followed the Community Weather-Balloon Launch Log Into the Payload They Took

parts.text: I unrolled balloon two at 5:07 a.m. and intern Cirrus was already clipping our numbered payload. The sheet said: ONE LAUNCH. SIGN THE LOG. PAYLOAD STAYS WITH THE KIT. I was thirty-five, club lead, holding a NOTAM that listed our flight. Cirrus shrugged. "Interns are the sky." I photographed the sheet, the log, and his tracker on our string. Then I asked for the launch log. At 5:15 the pad pinged why Cirrus's name was on our payload. I kept my voice pad-quiet and let the timestamp talk. A sheet is only a sheet until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The pad can see Cirrus's tracker on our string during our launch.

social.video_title: He clipped our numbered payload without the log — Part 1/2
social.description: Weather balloon, an intern on our string, a launch log he skipped. I logged the tracker. Would you have asked for the launch log?

parts.text: Cirrus called it a test until the pad asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the sheet, and the tracker still. The payload went back to our kit. Cirrus ran his own launch and told the next intern atmosphere was always about burst. Burst is a word interns use when a log exists. Launch policy now has a second line: INTERNS ARE NOT THE SKY. I keep our kit on a labeled bin. Cirrus brown-bags his jokes. The pad finally looks like a log, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Interns are not the sky — Part 2/2
social.description: Launch log, numbered payload, and a second line on the sheet. Was a test ever our string?
